speeches.speaker: Sussan Ley
speeches.brief: The Health Legislation Amendment (eHealth) Bill 2015 implements the government's $485 million eHealth commitment, renaming the personally controlled electronic health record as My Health Record and trialling opt-out participation arrangements in 2016. It also introduces criminal penalties for deliberate misuse of health information, establishes the Australian Commission for eHealth, disbands the National E-Health Transition Authority, and clarifies privacy definitions for health services and health information.

speeches.speaker: Catherine King
speeches.brief: The speaker argued the Health Legislation Amendment (eHealth) Bill 2015 is a belated government response after $215 million in cuts and two years of neglect, supporting the opt-out trials and name change to myHealth Record but warning against rushing implementation, while noting Labor’s prior investment and potential savings of $7.6 billion annually by 2020 and 5,000 lives saved each year.

speeches.speaker: Jane Prentice
speeches.brief: The Health Legislation Amendment (eHealth) Bill 2015 was supported, proposing trials of an opt-out model for electronic health records (renamed My Health Record) in selected regions, aiming to increase adoption from the current 10% rate, with added privacy safeguards and penalties for misuse.

speeches.speaker: Chris Bowen
speeches.brief: Opposition supports the thrust of the Health Legislation Amendment (eHealth) Bill 2015; the relevant shadow minister will elaborate further.

speeches.speaker: Stephen Jones
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that Labor introduced and expanded the personally controlled electronic health record (PCEHR) system, now renamed My Health Record, and criticised the government for cutting $215 million from the program and delaying progress for two years. The speaker supported the bill's opt-out trials and new criminal penalties for privacy breaches but called for further Senate scrutiny on privacy protections.

speeches.speaker: Brett Whiteley
speeches.brief: The Health Legislation Amendment (eHealth) Bill 2015 renames the PCEHR system to My Health Record, enables opt-out trials, and introduces new governance and penalties, aiming to reduce the 2.5% of hospital admissions from incomplete medication histories, the 36% of clinician visits wasting time locating information, and the 10% of avoidable lab tests, as health costs are projected to reach $86 billion by 2025.

speeches.speaker: Justine Elliot
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the intent of the bill to rename the eHealth record to myHealth record and enable opt-out trials in northern New South Wales and metropolitan Queensland, but called for further scrutiny of privacy provisions. They noted that Labor introduced the eHealth system, criticised the government for cutting $215 million in funding and delaying action, and cited that medication errors cause 190,000 hospital admissions annually costing $660 million.

speeches.speaker: Sussan Ley
speeches.brief: The Health Legislation Amendment (eHealth) Bill 2015 reboots the national electronic health record system as My Health Record, implements 2013 review recommendations, and schedules opt-out participation trials in 2016 to boost uptake from the current one in ten Australians.
